name: Kira Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a hydraulic shovel at an open-pit zinc mine, the big digger that loads the haul trucks. I sit up high, take a bite of the blasted rock, swing and dump it in the truck, around sixty trucks a shift when things go well. I'm still learning to read the muck pile, and the trainer, Graham, reckons I waste swings because I second-guess myself. What I love is getting into a rhythm where the trucks never wait.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about your life outside the pit.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Josh two years ago, he's a diesel fitter at the same mine. No kids yet, but we want them. Between us we've got close to a year of pay saved, and on weekends Josh and I run a little earthmoving business with a skid steer, doing driveways and house pads for farmers. I use AI every day to write quotes, sort invoices and study for my next ticket. There's plenty of mining work around, so we're not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. I'd still use it for the business, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but still handy, because it writes my quotes in five minutes instead of an hour. At work I'd say the hard work still gets done by people. Online I'd just post about the skid steer jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep getting better on the shovel and keep growing the weekend business. Nothing much changes, and that's okay. The zinc price is what I watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep the business going, and buy a second machine, maybe a small excavator, next year. Save for a house and kids in a couple of years. I'd do my next ticket so I can move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the weekend business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth of what I earn at the mine. It's not huge, but it's ours. The skid steer business Josh (my husband) and I run on weekends only brings in a fifth of my mine pay, but nobody can sack us from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zinc prices. And Josh's back, he's done some damage in the workshop. But we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd see as a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who work hard and learn will do fine, and the rest need to get on with it. At work I'd tell the crew to learn the systems. Online I'd share how I use AI for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The planning and dispatch work goes to software first, and I'd want to be the one who learns the fleet control screens. I'd rather be the woman in the control room running ten autonomous trucks than the one waiting for a robot to take my shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on the fleet management system straight away. I'd use AI more for the business, maybe get a booking tool online. And I'd buy that second machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's hands-on, a fitter, so he's safe for a good while. Robots break down and need fixing. He's the steady one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older blokes who won't touch a computer. But I'd tell them to learn, it's not that hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fast. Two years for the thinking, five for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should take responsibility and get ready, not wait for handouts. At work I'd tell the crew to learn what they can now. Online I'd keep sharing tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the control room job I wanted goes in 2028 too, because AGI can run the fleet itself. Then the shovel goes by 2031. With AGI by 2028, even the control room I was aiming for would be run by software before I got a seat in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the weekend business fast, because farmers still want someone they know. I'd save harder and maybe put off kids for a year. I'd help Josh get into robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be working to stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the business survive robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. But farmers trust people, and robots on a small job are expensive. I'd give it ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're working hard and we'll manage. My mum would pray for us, and that'd help too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then eight. That's more workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if people actually try. I'd say that at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can learn fleet control, then move into the business full time by 2034. Five years is enough to grow the weekend business into a full-time one before robots take my shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train on fleet systems, grow the business, buy a second machine. Have kids on schedule. Josh keeps fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on workers in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one or two. Probably people from the mine who lost jobs. I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with AI in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quotes, bookings, maybe planning the jobs. It'd let me run it without an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to get ready. People should learn and plan. I'd say it at work and church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's a good chance for me. Ten years means I could turn a weekend skid steer business into a proper company before robots take my seat on the shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your company look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three machines and a couple of workers. Josh would join full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still worrying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in small earthmoving, eventually. But by then I'd have time to adapt again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even my backup plan, the control room, goes away. What would help is training on the new systems and fewer rules for small businesses. My weekend skid steer business is my real safety net, more than any mine job or government plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small businesses. People like me can build something that lasts, if we're allowed to.

They run a **weekend business** doing earthmoving, and she uses AI every day for it.
She sees change as a **chance** and believes in hard work, not handouts.
She's **calm** in most scenarios but **anxious** if AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her control room backup plan would vanish.
